title: How Ice Cream Works
summary: Josh and Chuck run through ice cream: their personal favorites and favorite shops, the history of frozen dairy treats from ancient snow-and-honey ices through Roman emperors, Renaissance royalty, the first Paris cafe, early American ads and presidential recipes, and the rise of take-home ice cream with ice boxes. They cover the Johnson hand crank, soda fountains and the Sunday spelling story, ice cream in World War One and Two, and frozen yogurt. The science section explains ice cream as a colloid, the role of emulsifiers, the USDA ice cream definition (10% milk fat, 4.5 lb gallon), overrun and air, why salt lowers the freezing point in hand-cranked makers, the dasher and hardening, and making ice cream in plastic bags. The episode also covers the ice cream cone origin story (1904 St. Louis World's Fair, Italo Marchiony), Jacob Fussell, Penn State's ice cream course, consumption stats (New Zealand leads per capita), popular flavors, brain freeze, and a listener mail segment about a scientific method episode.

segments.title: Favorite ice cream flavors and shops
segments.summary: The hosts chat about their favorite ice cream flavors and brands, lactose sensitivity, Ben and Jerry's, and favorite ice cream parlors, including odd flavors like tuna gelato and heat-infused ice cream.

segments.title: Ancient and royal origins of ice cream
segments.summary: The episode introduces the history of frozen dairy treats, citing ancient snow and honey ices attributed to Alexander the Great, Roman emperors sending runners for snow, Marco Polo bringing ideas to Italy, English cream ice, and Catherine de Medici. Ice was a luxury for royalty until a Paris cafe sold ice cream to the public in 1660.

segments.title: Brain freeze
segments.summary: The hosts discuss brain freeze, describing a blood vessel from the brain to the roof of the mouth that constricts and causes pain, and suggested remedies such as pressing the tongue to the roof of the mouth.

segments.title: Early American ice cream and presidential recipes
segments.summary: Ice cream appears in American print in 1744 in a letter from a guest of Maryland's governor, and in a 1777 New York Gazette ad. George Washington and Thomas Jefferson had recipes and Dolley Madison served it at the White House. Joey Chestnut's eating record is mentioned.

segments.title: Ice boxes, take-home ice cream and the Johnson crank
segments.summary: Wholesale manufacturing grew around 1800, and ice boxes made take-home ice cream widespread, which boosted the industry. Nancy Johnson patented a hand-crank ice cream maker in the 1850s; she sold the patent cheaply and others copied it. Take-home ice cream still makes up most of the market.

segments.title: Soda fountains, the Sunday spelling and ice cream in wartime
segments.summary: Late nineteenth-century soda fountains created floats and Sundaes; the spelling change to Sundae followed religious criticism of Sunday indulgence. During World War I ice cream was deemed essential food and got sugar rations; during World War II the armed forces served ice cream to troops, including a Navy floating ice cream parlor. The Depression slowed sales.

segments.title: Frozen yogurt and the rise of health-conscious frozen treats
segments.summary: The hosts discuss frozen yogurt's growth in the seventies and later, Greek yogurt trends, and childhood memories of TCBY. Frozen yogurt is made by adding yogurt cultures during processing.

segments.title: Ice cream as a colloid and the role of emulsifiers
segments.summary: Ice cream is described as a colloid made of fat, sugar and milk mixed with air, held together by an emulsifier such as egg yolks, or stabilizers like xanthan gum in factories. Frozen yogurt and sherbet differ by ingredients and process. The USDA standard requires at least 10 percent milk fat, 6 percent non-fat milk solids, and a gallon weighing 4.5 pounds. Milk fat levels of 14 to 16 percent are considered ideal.

segments.title: How the freezing and churning process works
segments.summary: The hosts explain churning with a dasher that whips in air and prevents large ice crystals, the difference between soft serve and hardened ice cream, and how salt lowers the freezing point of the ice bath in hand-crank makers. A plastic bag ice cream recipe is mentioned, along with pasteurization.

segments.title: Overrun and cones
segments.summary: Overrun is the increase in volume from added air, with premium ice creams being denser and lower in overrun. The hosts talk about cone preferences and the waffle cone origin at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, which popularized cones, while Italo Marchiony is credited with the cone.

segments.title: Jacob Fussell, ice cream courses and industry stats
segments.summary: Jacob Fussell started the first wholesale ice cream operation in Baltimore after having extra cream. Penn State and Wisconsin offer ice cream courses; Ben and Jerry's met at Penn State. The US produces about twenty quarts per capita, and New Zealand leads consumption at 7.5 gallons per person versus 5.5 for Americans. Vanilla is the most popular flavor, and green tea ranked high in a survey.

segments.title: Listener mail: scientific method and spelling Jerry's name
segments.summary: A listener named Danny, an astronomy and physics graduate, praises the earlier scientific method episode and promotes his astrophysics blog. Another listener is greeted, and the hosts note the show receives a few hundred emails a week.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and website contact details and direct listeners to HowStuffWorks.com.
